title: Laptop hardware: what's different and why it matters
summary: SODIMM, M.2, and the parts you'll actually be asked to replace.
body:
## Everything is smaller, and that's the whole story

A laptop is a desktop with the same jobs and none of the room. Almost every A+ laptop question comes down to knowing the *small-form-factor* version of a part you already recognize.

### Memory

Laptops use **SODIMM** (Small Outline DIMM) rather than the full-length DIMMs desktops use. They're physically shorter and keyed differently, so you can't accidentally fit a desktop stick.

- **DDR4 SODIMM** — 260 pins
- **DDR5 SODIMM** — 262 pins

The pin counts differ from their desktop cousins (DDR4 DIMM is 288 pins), so a slot only accepts one generation. If a memory upgrade won't seat, the first suspect is a **generation or form-factor mismatch**, not a bad module.

### Storage

Modern laptops overwhelmingly use **M.2** drives. Two things trip people up:

- **M.2 is a form factor, not an interface.** An M.2 slot can carry either **SATA** or **NVMe** signaling. A drive and slot can physically fit and still not work if the slot only wired one of the two.
- **Keying** (the notch position — B key, M key, B+M) tells you what a slot supports. An NVMe drive is usually M-keyed; a SATA M.2 is often B+M.

### The parts you actually replace

Field-replaceable on most laptops: RAM, the M.2 or 2.5" drive, the **battery**, the **Wi-Fi card**, and sometimes the keyboard. The **display assembly** — panel, backlight, and often the antenna and webcam — is treated as one unit; you rarely replace the panel alone.

> Exam habit: when a laptop symptom involves wireless, remember the **Wi-Fi antenna wires run up through the hinges into the display bezel**. A screen replacement that leaves Wi-Fi weak usually means an antenna lead wasn't reconnected.

### Display technologies

You'll be asked to compare panel types:

- **TN** — fastest response, cheapest, worst color and viewing angles.
- **IPS** — best color accuracy and viewing angles, slightly slower.
- **VA** — best contrast, a middle ground on everything else.
- **OLED** — per-pixel lighting, true blacks, risk of burn-in.

And know that the **inverter** (which powered older CCFL backlights) is a legacy concept — LED-backlit panels don't use one, so a modern dim-screen problem points at the backlight LEDs or the panel, not an inverter.

title: Mobile connectivity: cellular, Bluetooth, and hotspots
summary: The radios in a phone and the settings that break them.
body:
## Three radios, three failure modes

Mobile devices juggle several radios at once, and A+ likes to test whether you can tell which one a symptom belongs to.

### Cellular

- A **SIM** (or eSIM) identifies the device to the carrier. "No SIM" or "not registered" errors point here.
- **Airplane mode** kills *all* radios at once. It's the single fastest way to explain "nothing wireless works, everything else is fine."
- **PRL** (Preferred Roaming List) and baseband/radio firmware updates are carrier-side fixes for a phone that connects but can't get data.

### Bluetooth

Bluetooth has to be **paired** before it works, and pairing is where problems live:

1. Make the device **discoverable**.
2. Initiate pairing from the other device.
3. Confirm the **PIN or passkey** if prompted.
4. Test the connection.

If a previously working device won't reconnect, **removing (forgetting) the pairing and re-pairing** clears most stale-pairing faults.

### Hotspots and tethering

A phone can share its cellular data three ways:

- **Wi-Fi hotspot** — the phone becomes an access point.
- **Bluetooth tethering** — slower, but very low power.
- **USB tethering** — fastest and charges the phone at the same time.

> Exam habit: "hotspot works but the laptop can't reach it" is usually the hotspot's **maximum connected-device limit** or a **band mismatch** (an older laptop that only sees 2.4 GHz while the hotspot broadcasts 5 GHz).

title: Ports and protocols worth memorizing
summary: The port numbers A+ asks about, grouped so they stick.
body:
## Learn them in pairs and groups, not as a flat list

Rote-memorizing 20 port numbers is miserable and doesn't stick. Group them by what they do.

### Web and its secure twin

| Service | Port | Note |
|---|---|---|
| HTTP | 80 | Plain web |
| HTTPS | 443 | TLS-encrypted web |

Almost every "secure version" rides a different port — this pairing is the pattern to internalize.

### Remote access

| Service | Port | Note |
|---|---|---|
| SSH | 22 | Encrypted remote shell |
| Telnet | 23 | **Unencrypted** — legacy, avoid |
| RDP | 3389 | Windows Remote Desktop |

SSH (22) and Telnet (23) sit right next to each other and do the same job; the exam loves that SSH is the secure one.

### Mail

| Service | Port | Direction |
|---|---|---|
| SMTP | 25 | Sending |
| POP3 | 110 | Retrieving (download) |
| IMAP | 143 | Retrieving (sync) |

### Naming, addressing, and file sharing

| Service | Port |
|---|---|
| DNS | 53 |
| DHCP | 67 / 68 |
| SMB (file sharing) | 445 |
| LDAP | 389 |

> Exam habit: **DNS is 53**. It shows up constantly, both as a port question and as the answer to "I can reach a site by IP but not by name." Burn 53 into memory first.

title: IP addressing and what APIPA is telling you
summary: Private ranges, DHCP, and reading 169.254 as a diagnosis.
body:
## An address is a diagnosis

The single most useful networking skill for the exam — and the job — is reading an IP address as a clue about what went wrong.

### Private ranges (RFC 1918)

These never route on the public internet; a home or office LAN uses them behind NAT:

- **10.0.0.0** – 10.255.255.255 (a /8)
- **172.16.0.0** – 172.31.255.255 (a /12)
- **192.168.0.0** – 192.168.255.255 (a /16)

Seeing one of these on a client is normal and expected.

### APIPA — the address that means "DHCP failed"

If a client is set to obtain an address automatically but **can't reach a DHCP server**, it assigns itself one from:

> **169.254.0.0 – 169.254.255.255**

This is **APIPA** (Automatic Private IP Addressing). An APIPA address is a symptom, not a setting. It means:

- The DHCP server is down or unreachable, **or**
- A cable/switch problem is cutting the client off from it, **or**
- The client and server are on different segments with no DHCP relay.

A machine with a 169.254 address can talk to *other* APIPA machines on the same segment but has no gateway and no DNS — so "local network works, internet doesn't" with a 169.254 address is a classic DHCP-failure signature.

### Loopback

**127.0.0.1** (IPv4) always refers to the local machine. Pinging it tests that the TCP/IP stack itself is alive — if that fails, the problem is the OS's networking, not any cable.

### Static vs dynamic

Most clients get addresses from **DHCP**. Servers, printers, and network gear are often **static** (or DHCP reservations) so their address never changes. A printer that "moves" and breaks everyone's print queue is usually a static device that got a DHCP address, or vice versa.

title: SOHO networks, VPNs, and the tools that diagnose them
summary: What a small office/home office network is made of, how a VPN fits in, and the tools that troubleshoot the wiring itself.
body:
## One box doing four jobs

A SOHO (small office/home office) network is almost always built around one consumer-grade device doing several jobs at once: **router**, **switch**, **wireless access point**, and **firewall**, all in a single case. On the exam, when a scenario describes "the home router," it's implicitly all four of those roles — know which role a described symptom belongs to. No wireless clients connecting is an AP problem; nothing reaching the internet is a router/WAN problem; wired devices not seeing each other is a switch problem.

### VPNs: extending the private network over the internet

A **VPN (Virtual Private Network)** wraps traffic in an encrypted tunnel across an untrusted network — normally the public internet — so the remote end behaves as if it were plugged into the private LAN.

Two shapes show up on the exam:

- **Client-to-site (remote-access) VPN** — a VPN app on one device connects that single user in. This is the shape for an individual remote or home worker reaching the office.
- **Site-to-site VPN** — an always-on tunnel between two routers/gateways, joining two entire networks (e.g., a branch office to headquarters). Every device behind each end reaches the other transparently, with no per-device app.

> Exam habit: "one remote employee needs secure access" → client-to-site. "Two office locations need to act as one network" → site-to-site.

### Networking tools: what each one actually tests

SOHO troubleshooting leans on a small physical toolkit, and the exam tests the tool as much as the symptom:

| Tool | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| **Crimper** | Attaches an RJ45 connector onto the end of a loose cable |
| **Cable tester** | Verifies a cable's pinout end-to-end — flags opens, shorts, and miswired pairs |
| **Wi-Fi analyzer** | Scans nearby channels and signal strength — the tool for diagnosing wireless interference or planning AP placement |

A punchdown tool (for seating wire into a wall jack) is the cousin of a crimper — crimper for loose cable ends, punchdown for jacks and patch panels. Don't confuse "which tool terminates a cable" (crimper/punchdown) with "which tool tells you if a cable is good" (cable tester) — they get tested as a pair.

Two more tools round out the kit: a **cable stripper** removes the outer jacket before a crimp or punchdown (the prep step those two tools depend on), and a **network tap** is inserted inline on a live link to copy traffic for a packet analyzer, without disrupting the connection itself — different job from a cable tester, which checks the cable's wiring, not the traffic on it.

title: Server roles, internet appliances, and legacy/embedded systems
summary: What each networked host actually does, matched to the acronym the exam names it by.
body:
## A network is a collection of hosts doing specific jobs

The exam expects you to recognize each server role and appliance by name and match it to what it does — most of this is naming discipline, not deep configuration.

### Server roles

| Role | Job |
|---|---|
| DNS server | Resolves names to IP addresses |
| DHCP server | Hands out IP configuration to clients |
| Fileshare server | Hosts shared folders/files over the network |
| Print server | Queues and routes print jobs to shared printers |
| Mail server | Sends/receives email (SMTP/IMAP/POP3) |
| Syslog server | Centrally collects log messages from other devices |
| Web server | Serves HTTP/HTTPS content |
| AAA server | Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting — verifies identity, decides access, and records what was done |
| Database server | Hosts structured data that applications query |
| NTP server | Keeps every device's clock synchronized |

> Exam habit: "every device on the network needs to agree on the current time" → NTP. "A central place all the switches and firewalls send their log messages" → syslog.

### Internet appliances

- **Spam gateway** — filters incoming mail for spam/phishing before it reaches the mail server.
- **UTM (Unified Threat Management)** — bundles multiple security functions (firewall, antivirus, content filtering, intrusion prevention) into one appliance, trading some specialization for simpler management.
- **Load balancer** — spreads client requests across multiple servers so no single one is overwhelmed.
- **Proxy server** — makes requests on a client's behalf, enabling caching, content filtering, and hiding internal addresses from the destination.

### Legacy/embedded systems and IoT

- **SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition)** — monitors and controls physical industrial processes (utilities, manufacturing). Often built on old, rarely-patched systems, which is exactly why it's normally isolated on its own segmented network rather than exposed alongside general office traffic.
- **IoT devices** — smart thermostats, cameras, sensors, and similar network-connected embedded devices. Same isolation principle as SCADA: segment them off the main network so a compromised smart device isn't a stepping stone to everything else.

title: RAID levels and what each one is buying you
summary: 0, 1, 5, 10 — the trade between speed, redundancy, and capacity.
body:
## Every RAID level is a trade

RAID combines multiple drives into one logical volume. Each level trades among three things: **speed**, **redundancy**, and **usable capacity**. Know what each one sacrifices.

### RAID 0 — striping

Data is split across drives, so reads and writes are fast. **No redundancy at all** — if any one drive dies, the whole array is lost.

- Minimum drives: 2
- Usable capacity: 100%
- Fault tolerance: **none**

RAID 0 is pure performance. The name is a trap — "0" means zero redundancy.

### RAID 1 — mirroring

Every drive holds an identical copy. Survives a drive failure with no data loss.

- Minimum drives: 2
- Usable capacity: 50%
- Fault tolerance: one drive

### RAID 5 — striping with parity

Data and **parity** are spread across all drives. Can rebuild after **one** drive fails using the parity.

- Minimum drives: 3
- Usable capacity: (n − 1) drives
- Fault tolerance: one drive

RAID 5 is the classic "balanced" choice — good capacity, good reads, survives one failure.

### RAID 10 — a mirror of stripes

Combines 1 and 0: mirrored pairs that are then striped. Fast **and** redundant, at the cost of half your capacity.

- Minimum drives: 4
- Usable capacity: 50%
- Fault tolerance: one drive per mirrored pair

> Exam habit: match the level to the *requirement in the question*. "Maximum performance, data is disposable" → **0**. "Survive a drive failure, only two drives" → **1**. "Balance capacity and redundancy across several drives" → **5**. "Best of both, budget allows" → **10**.

title: Power supplies: wattage, rails, and connectors
summary: Sizing a PSU and the connectors you have to recognize.
body:
## The part most likely to kill other parts

A failing power supply doesn't just stop working — it can behave intermittently and take other components with it. A+ expects you to size one correctly and recognize its connectors.

### Wattage: add up the load, then leave headroom

The PSU has to supply the **sum** of everything's draw, with margin. The single biggest consumer in most builds is the **GPU**, which is why a new graphics card is the most common reason an existing PSU becomes inadequate.

Signs of an **undersized or failing** PSU:

- Random reboots or shutdowns **under load** (gaming, rendering) but stable at idle
- The system won't POST with a new high-draw card installed
- Capacitor/coil noise or a burning smell

> Exam habit: "stable at idle, reboots under load, just added a GPU" is almost always **insufficient PSU wattage** or **missing PCIe power connectors** — not RAM, not the drive.

### Connectors to recognize

| Connector | Powers |
|---|---|
| 24-pin (20+4) | Motherboard main power |
| 8-pin (4+4) EPS | CPU power |
| 6/8-pin PCIe | Graphics card |
| SATA power | Drives, some fans |
| Molex | Legacy peripherals |

A modern GPU needs **specific 6- or 8-pin PCIe connectors** — verify both the total wattage *and* that the PSU has the right connectors before an upgrade.

### Voltage and safety

A PSU with a **voltage selector switch** (115V / 230V) must match the wall supply — the wrong setting damages hardware. And because PSUs hold charge, they're on the short list of parts you **don't open**; you replace them as a unit.

title: Peripherals: printers, scanners, and what breaks on each
summary: Printer technologies and their tell-tale failure symptoms, plus scanner basics.
body:
## Match the printer technology to the symptom

A+ printer questions almost always give a symptom and expect you to name the failing part — and the right part depends on which printer technology it is.

### Laser printers

Toner is fused onto the page with heat and pressure, using an imaging drum that's charged, exposed, and developed one page at a time:

- **Faded or smudged output that rubs off** — the **fuser** isn't melting toner onto the page properly.
- **A repeating mark or streak at a fixed interval down the page** — a scratched or dirty **imaging drum** (often integrated with the toner cartridge). "Repeating" is the keyword that points at the drum, not the fuser.
- **Paper jams or misfeeds** — worn **pickup rollers**.

### Inkjet printers

Liquid ink is sprayed through a print head — no fuser, no drum:

- **Streaky or faded output** on a freshly installed cartridge — low ink, or a clogged **print head** nozzle; most inkjets have a built-in head-cleaning/alignment utility to try first.
- Inkjets are cheaper per page for low volume but far more expensive per page at high volume than laser — a common "which printer should this office buy" scenario question.

### Thermal printers

No ink or toner at all — a heating element burns the image directly into heat-sensitive paper. Common in receipt printers.

- **Faded or blank output with a fresh paper roll loaded backwards** — thermal paper is one-sided; if it's in upside down, nothing prints.
- The heating element itself, and the paper-feed mechanism, are the two things that fail.

### Impact (dot-matrix) printers

A print head physically strikes an ink ribbon against the page — loud, but the only technology that works with **carbon-copy / multi-part forms**, since it makes a physical impression through multiple sheets.

### Installing and sharing printers

- **Local** printers connect directly (USB) to one machine; **network** printers get their own IP and are shared to many.
- Windows needs the right **driver** for the model — a generic/incompatible driver is a common cause of garbled or missing output after an install.
- A shared local printer depends on the **host PC being on** — a frequent "why can't anyone print" answer when the host machine was shut down or slept.

### Scanners

- **Flatbed** — one page (or a book) at a time, on glass. Best image quality.
- **ADF (automatic document feeder)** — feeds a stack of pages automatically; some support **duplex** scanning (both sides in one pass) either with two sensors or by flipping the page mechanically.

title: Deploying and configuring a printer, before anything goes wrong
summary: Setup, drivers, sharing, security, and network scanning — the configuration side, distinct from later maintenance.
body:
## Setup decisions now save troubleshooting calls later

### Unboxing and setup

Before connecting anything: pick a stable, ventilated location (laser printers exhaust heat and ozone), remove all shipping tape/inserts from the toner or print-head carriage, and let an inkjet's ink system initialize before printing.

### Drivers and firmware

Use the driver built for the specific OS and printer model — a generic or mismatched driver is a common cause of garbled output. Printers also ship **firmware**, updated separately from the driver, which can fix connectivity bugs or add features the driver alone can't.

**PCL vs. PostScript** are the two dominant print languages a driver can target: **PCL (Printer Command Language)** is faster and simpler, common for everyday business printing; **PostScript** handles complex graphics and precise page layout more faithfully, which is why graphic design and publishing workflows prefer it.

### Connectivity and sharing

- **Local** — direct USB connection to one PC.
- **Network** — Ethernet or wireless, with its own IP address, reachable by many clients directly.
- **Printer share** — one PC shares its locally-connected printer over the network; depends on that host PC staying on.
- **Print server** — a dedicated device or service queues and manages jobs for shared printers, without depending on any one user's PC being awake.

### Configuration settings

**Duplex** (auto two-sided printing), **orientation** (portrait/landscape), **tray settings** (which paper size/type/source), and **quality** (draft vs. high quality, trading speed for output fidelity) are the settings a scenario question expects you to pick correctly for a described job.

### Printer security

- **User authentication** — require sign-in before releasing a job, so print jobs aren't picked up by the wrong person.
- **Badging** — release a queued job only when the user badges in at the printer itself.
- **Audit logs** — record who printed what and when.
- **Secured prints** — a job holds in the queue, encrypted or PIN-protected, until the user is physically present to release it — the standard fix for sensitive documents sitting exposed in an output tray.

### Network scan services

A multifunction device's scanner can deliver a scanned document three ways: **email** (scan-to-email, sent directly from the device), **SMB** (scan-to-folder, dropped onto a network share), or **cloud services** (scan directly to a cloud storage account). Which one to use depends on where the user actually needs the file to end up.

title: Cloud models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, and the shared responsibility line
summary: Who manages what, and where your responsibility starts.
body:
## The difference is *who manages what*

The cloud service models are a single idea seen at three depths: the more the provider manages, the less you control — and the less you're responsible for.

### IaaS — Infrastructure as a Service

The provider gives you **virtual hardware**: compute, storage, networking. You install and manage the OS and everything above it. Think of a bare virtual machine you're handed the keys to.

*You manage:* OS, patches, runtime, apps, data.

### PaaS — Platform as a Service

The provider manages the OS and runtime; you just deploy **your application and data**. You don't patch the server — you push code.

*You manage:* your app, your data.

### SaaS — Software as a Service

The provider manages **everything**; you just use the finished software through a browser. Email like Microsoft 365, or a CRM, are SaaS.

*You manage:* your data and your user accounts, essentially nothing else.

> A one-line mnemonic: **IaaS = you get a server, PaaS = you get a platform, SaaS = you get software.** Each step up hands more of the stack to the provider.

### Deployment models

Separately from *what* is delivered, there's *where*:

- **Public cloud** — shared provider infrastructure (AWS, Azure).
- **Private cloud** — dedicated to one organization.
- **Hybrid** — a mix, with workloads moving between them.
- **Community** — shared by organizations with common needs.

### Other terms A+ uses

- **Elasticity / rapid scaling** — resources grow and shrink on demand.
- **Measured service** — you pay for exactly what you use (metered).
- **Resource pooling** — many customers share one physical pool, isolated logically.
- **High availability** — the service survives individual component failures.

title: Virtualization concepts: hypervisors, VMs, and VDI
summary: What actually runs a virtual machine, and how VDI differs from just having a VM.
body:
## The cloud models are about *delivery*; this is about the *mechanism*

The previous lesson covered IaaS/PaaS/SaaS — who manages what. This one covers the technology underneath: what actually runs a virtual machine.

### Hypervisor types

A **hypervisor** is the software layer that creates and runs virtual machines, giving each one virtual CPU, RAM, storage, and network hardware carved out of the physical host.

- **Type 1 (bare-metal)** — runs directly on the server hardware, with no host operating system underneath it. Examples: ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox. This is what datacenters and serious virtualization hosts use — no OS overhead between the hypervisor and the hardware.
- **Type 2 (hosted)** — runs as an application on top of a normal host OS. Examples: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, Parallels. This is what you run on a laptop to spin up a test VM alongside your regular desktop.

> Exam habit: "runs directly on the hardware, no host OS" → Type 1. "Installed as a program inside Windows/macOS" → Type 2.

### Sizing a virtualization host

Every VM's virtual RAM, vCPUs, and storage come out of the physical host's real resources, plus overhead for the hypervisor itself. A host that's fine running two VMs can fail to start a third — not because anything is broken, but because the host is simply out of RAM or storage to allocate. "A new VM won't power on" is very often a resource-availability question, not a configuration error.

### Containers, briefly

Containers are a lighter alternative: they share the host OS kernel and isolate at the process level, instead of each one booting a full guest OS the way a VM does. That makes them faster to start and lighter on resources — but every container on a host is tied to that host's kernel, unlike a VM, which carries its own complete OS.

### VDI — desktop virtualization

**VDI (Virtual Desktop Infrastructure)** takes the VM idea and applies it to end-user desktops: each employee's "PC" is actually a VM running in the datacenter, and their physical device — often a cheap **thin client** — just streams the display and forwards input.

Why an organization does this: IT patches, backs up, and secures **one** central set of desktop images instead of hundreds of physical machines scattered around a building. If a thin client breaks, swapping it loses nothing — the actual desktop and data never lived on it.

> Exam habit: don't confuse VDI with IaaS. IaaS is a cloud company renting you infrastructure; VDI is centralizing *desktops* specifically, and can run entirely on an organization's own on-prem hardware.

title: The six-step troubleshooting methodology
summary: The process A+ tests directly — in order, and why the order matters.
body:
## The exam tests the *order*, not just the steps

This is the single most reliably tested procedure on the exam, and questions almost always hinge on **what comes next** from a given point. Learn it as a sequence.

### The six steps

1. **Identify the problem.** Gather information, question the user, and — critically — **back up before making changes**. Reproduce the problem if you can.
2. **Establish a theory of probable cause.** Question the obvious. Consider everything from the simplest explanation up.
3. **Test the theory to determine the cause.** If the theory is confirmed, move on. If not, form a new theory — or **escalate**.
4. **Establish a plan of action** to resolve the problem, and implement it.
5. **Verify full system functionality** and, if applicable, implement **preventive measures** so it doesn't recur.
6. **Document** findings, actions, and outcomes.

### Why each boundary matters

- **Backing up sits in step 1**, before any change. This catches people out — the temptation is to jump to a fix, but the methodology puts data protection first.
- **Testing the theory (3) comes before the plan (4).** You don't build a fix around a guess; you confirm the cause first. "You have a theory, what next?" is *test it*, not *fix it*.
- **Verify (5) comes before document (6).** You confirm the fix actually worked before you write it up — documenting a fix you never verified is how a "resolved" ticket bounces back.

> Exam habit: when a question drops you at one step and asks for the next, don't reason from the technical situation — recite the sequence. The answer is whatever step follows, every time.

title: Reading POST failures and boot problems
summary: Beeps, no-POST, and where a boot actually dies.
body:
## Where in the boot did it die?

Boot problems feel chaotic until you place *where* the failure happened. A machine powers on, runs **POST** (Power-On Self-Test), hands off to the **boot device**, then loads the OS. Each stage fails differently.

### No power at all

No lights, no fans. Work outward from the wall: power cable, PSU switch and voltage selector, the motherboard power connectors, then the power button header. This is a **power delivery** problem, not a boot problem.

### Powers on, no display, no POST

Fans spin but nothing appears and it never beeps normally. Suspect the parts POST checks first:

- **RAM** — reseat it; a single stick in the first slot is the classic isolation test.
- **GPU / display** — reseat, confirm the monitor and cable.
- **CPU / motherboard** — last, and hardest.

**POST beep codes** and motherboard diagnostic LEDs tell you which subsystem failed before video is even available. A repeating memory beep pattern points straight at RAM.

### POSTs, but can't find an OS

You see POST, then **"No boot device"**, "Operating system not found," or **"Inaccessible boot device."** POST passed, so the hardware basics are fine — the problem is between firmware and OS:

- Wrong **boot order** in UEFI/BIOS (booting an empty USB or the wrong disk).
- The boot drive isn't detected — a **loose SATA/power cable** or a failed drive.
- Corrupt bootloader or partition table.

### Boots, then fails loading Windows

Getting into the bootloader and then failing — a **BSOD**, a boot loop, or **"Bootmgr is missing"** — is an OS-level problem (drivers, corrupt system files, a bad update), not hardware. This is where Startup Repair and Safe Mode come in.

> Exam habit: the diagnostic question is always **"how far did it get?"** No POST → hardware POST checks (RAM/GPU/CPU). POSTs but no OS → boot order and the drive. Loads Windows and crashes → the OS. Placing the failure narrows the cause before you touch anything.

title: The physical troubleshooting toolkit
summary: Multimeter, cable tester, loopback plug — what each one actually proves.
body:
## Rule things out with a tool, not a guess

Hardware and network troubleshooting has a small set of physical tools, and the exam tests what each one specifically proves — not just "which tool fixes this."

| Tool | Proves |
|---|---|
| **Multimeter** | Whether an outlet, cable, or PSU rail is actually carrying voltage, and whether a connection has continuity |
| **Cable tester** | Whether a cable's pinout is correct end-to-end — catches opens, shorts, and miswired pairs a visual check would miss |
| **Loopback plug** | Whether a NIC or switch port itself works, by wiring the port's transmit pins back to its receive pins — no live network needed |
| **Toner probe (tone generator + probe)** | Which physical cable run corresponds to which jack, by injecting a tone at one end and tracing it at a patch panel |

### Reading the symptom to the tool

- **A PC won't power on at all — no lights, no fans.** Before opening the case further, a **multimeter** on the outlet and PSU output confirms whether power is actually the problem, rather than guessing and swapping parts.
- **A specific port or NIC is suspected bad, but there's no live network to test against.** A **loopback plug** isolates the port itself from everything else in the path.
- **A cable run works intermittently or not at all, and the wiring itself is the suspect.** A **cable tester** checks the pinout; a bad crimp or a miswired pair shows up immediately.
- **A cable disappears into a wall or a bundle of dozens of others, and you need to find its other end.** A **toner probe** traces it — inject the tone at one end, sweep the probe at the patch panel until it beeps.

> Exam habit: these questions are almost always phrased as "which tool should the technician use," with the symptom doing the work of telling you which one. Match the *proves* column above to the scenario, not the *sounds most technical* option.
